verdict: Across 4,956 MEASURED single-point interface mutations (SKEMPI, 345 complexes), the pattern that governs whether a mutation changes a PPI is clear and structural: (1) POSITION carries the energy — buried CORE interface residues have mean |ΔΔG| 1.92 kcal/mol with 38% being hotspots, while RIM/surface mutations average 0.84 and rarely matter — binding energy is concentrated in a few buried residues (the classic hotspot/O-ring law, reproduced here). (2) IDENTITY matters — the strongest hotspot residues are the large/charged/aromatic ones (L, K, W, E); small/flexible ones are weak. (3) A mutation weakens binding through BOTH a higher association barrier and a less stable bound state (32% barrier-dominated), so the on/off rates separate an encounter-barrier effect from an induced-fit/stability effect. (4) From residue change + interface depth ALONE we predict the measured ΔΔG at complex-held-out Pearson 0.36 — modest but real, and honest for these SIMPLE features (residue change + coarse position); full structural predictors (mCSM-PPI2, BeAtMuSiC) reach ~0.5-0.6 on blind splits by adding real interface burial and contacts, so there is headroom by fetching the complex geometry. interface_depth + volume/hydropathy change are the top features. SO: for the single-nucleotide-mutation goal, we CAN flag which interface positions are load-bearing (core, aromatic/charged, high predicted ΔΔG) and whether a variant there will hit the barrier or the stability — a genuine near-field structural capability. HONEST LIMITS: r~0.36 means we RANK and TRIAGE interface variants, we don't nail every ΔΔG; SKEMPI is biased to well-studied complexes; and this needs a solved/predicted COMPLEX structure to place the residue at an interface (no complex -> no call).
